ABSTRACT: Herein, we report a method for enantioselective vinylogous addition of enones to alkoxyallenes enabled by synergistic
borane/palladium catalysis. The inductive efect provided by borane coordination to the ketone was essential for closing the gap
between the conditions needed for the generation of a dienolate and those needed for initiation of the palladium catalytic cycle by
protonation of the metal catalyst. Furthermore, we accomplished the first example of stereodivergent synthesis with chiral borane/
transition-metal catalysts.

Next, we investigated the scope with respect to the enone
by using benzyloxyallene (2a) as the coupling partner (Table
3). Aryl ketones with various substituents on the benzene ring
attached to the carbonyl group were tolerated, giving
corresponding products 4b−4m. Functionality such as
halogen atoms (4d−4f, 4m) and ester (4h), vinyl (4i), and
alkynyl (4j) groups were retained. Moreover, the benzene ring
could be replaced by a 2-naphthyl (4n), 5-benzofuranyl (4o),
5-benzothiophenyl (4p), or 2-thienyl (4q) group. However,
little of the desired product was obtained when the aryl group
was replaced with an alkynyl or alkyl group under the standard
conditions (data not shown). Interestingly, however, we found
that these substrates could be converted if
\mathrm { B } ( \mathrm { C } _ { 6 } \mathrm { F } _ { 5 } ) .
was
replaced with one of the chiral spirobicyclic bisborane
catalysts developed in our group (CAT1 or CAT2).<sup>21</sup> With
these catalysts, reactions of alkynyl-substituted enones gave
the target products (4r−4t) with high enantioselectivities, and
a cyclohexyl-substituted ketone gave 4u in 69% yield with
82% ee. The activity of CAT1 and CAT2 in these reactions is
similar, with the diference lying in their enantioselectivity. A
matched/mismatched efect also impacts the enantioselectiv-
ity. For example, the use of ent-CAT2 with L1 in the reaction
of 1r aforded 4r in 71% yield and 73% ee. Notably, even
though ketone 1u has an additional enolization site on the
cyclohexyl group, no side product resulting from enolate
addition at this site was detected. However, replacing the
cyclohexyl group in 1u with methyl or t-butyl groups results in
no reaction or the formation of only trace amounts of
products.
Subsequently, we tested enones with various α and β
substituents. When the α substituent was ethyl, n-butyl,
benzyl, cyclopropyl, or alkynyl, corresponding products 4v−
4z, respectively, were obtained in 79−90% yields with 84−
92% ee. However, the ee dropped to 76% when the ketone
had an α-hydrogen atom (4aa). Interestingly, β-disubstituted
enone 1bb was also reactive, giving 4bb in 42% yield with
90% ee, despite the increased steric hindrance. When we
replaced the β-methyl group with a benzyl or n-butyl group,
products 4cc and 4dd, which have adjacent stereogenic
centers, were formed in good yields but with poor
diastereoselectivity. Notably, no byproducts generated by
reactions at the α position of the enones were detected in any
of the above-mentioned reactions in Tables 2 and 3, perhaps
because of the steric bulk of the borane catalyst. The absolute
configuration of 4h was determined by X-ray single-crystal
analysis (CCDC 2401879), whereas the configurations of the

In summary, we have developed a method for regio- and
enantioselective coupling of enones with alkoxyallenes with
synergistic borane/palladium catalysis. The strong inductive
efect of coordination of the borane catalyst to the carbonyl
group of the enone enabled trialkylamine-promoted enoliza-
tion, a process that is otherwise impossible because of the high
pK values of these compounds. The resulting protonated
trialkylamine could protonate the palladium catalyst to initiate
the palladium catalytic cycle. In this way, the pK limit for
carbonyl pronucleophiles in palladium-catalyzed coupling
reactions with unsaturated hydrocarbons has been increased
to approximately 26. Furthermore, by combining chiral
spirobicyclic bisborane catalysts with chiral palladium
catalysts, we accomplished stereodivergent synthesis. We
believe that such synergistic borane/transition-metal catalytic
systems could push the boundaries of well-established catalytic
systems with transition metals, thereby leading to the
discovery of new reactions.
